Italian astronomer, physicist, engineer, and [[Polymath|polymath]]. Born in Pisa, then part of the Duchy of Florence, the son of the lutenist and music theorist Vincenzo Galilei, he enrolled in 1580 at the University of Pisa for a medical degree. Galileo has been called the father of observational astronomy, classical physics, the scientific method, and modern science.

He studied speed and velocity, gravity and free fall, inertia, and projectile motion, and described the properties of the pendulum. In 1609 he improved the refracting [[Telescope|telescope]], reaching magnifications up to 30 times. With it he observed the stars of the [[Milky Way]], the phases of Venus, the four largest [[Moons of Jupiter|satellites of Jupiter]], Saturn's rings, lunar craters, and sunspots. These findings, detailed in *Sidereus Nuncius* (1610), supported the heliocentric model of [[Nicolaus Copernicus|Copernicus]].

His championing of heliocentrism met opposition from within the [[Catholic Church]] and from some astronomers. The Roman Inquisition investigated the matter in 1615 and concluded that his opinions contradicted accepted Biblical interpretations. His *Dialogue Concerning the Two Chief World Systems* (1632) appeared to dispute and satirize Pope Urban VIII, alienating both the Pope and the Jesuits, who had strongly supported him. Tried by the Inquisition, he was found "vehemently suspect of heresy", forced to recant, and kept under house arrest for the rest of his life. During that time he wrote *Discourses and Mathematical Demonstrations Relating to Two New Sciences* (1638), primarily on kinematics and the [[Strength of materials|strength of materials]]. His emphasis on mathematics and experiment influenced later scientists, among them [[Isaac Newton]].

Wagering of something of value ("the stakes") on a random event with the intent of winning something else of value, where instances of strategy are discounted. Gambling requires three elements: consideration (an amount wagered), risk (chance), and a prize. The outcome may be immediate, as with a roll of dice or a spin of a roulette wheel, or may take longer, as with wagers on a sports season. "Gaming" typically refers to gambling specifically permitted by law, though the distinction is not universally observed. The legal gambling market totaled an estimated $335 billion in 2009. By one estimate, roughly 46% of adults gamble in a year and about 2% develop problem gambling.

Gambling dates back at least to the Paleolithic period. In [[Mesopotamia]], the earliest six-sided dice date to about 3000 BC. Gambling houses were widespread in China in the first millennium BC, and playing cards appeared there in the 9th century. [[Poker]] derives from the Persian game As-Nas, dating to the 17th century. The first known [[Casino|casino]], the Ridotto, began operating in 1638 in Venice. [[Elizabeth I]] chartered a lottery drawn in 1569. By the early 20th century gambling was almost uniformly outlawed in the United States, which helped spur organized crime; laws relaxed in the late 20th century.

Many jurisdictions ban gambling or regulate it by licensing vendors, which generally produces gambling tourism and illegal gambling elsewhere. Legal gambling provides significant government revenue, as in [[Monaco]] and Macau, China. In many American states one must be over 21 to enter a casino but may buy a lottery ticket at 18. Contracts of [[Insurance|insurance]] resemble wagers but are distinguished in law because either party has an interest in the outcome beyond the financial terms.

Activity defined by a challenge and a set of rules, typically done for enjoyment, competition, or development. Games may be played informally or in professional competitive settings before audiences. Popular formats include board games, card games, video games, and sports, which are distinguished from unstructured play by having rules. Scholars have long debated the essence of games, and no single definition has achieved universal acceptance.

[[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] argued in *Philosophical Investigations* that play, rules, and competition each fail to define games, and concluded that the term covers disparate activities bearing only family resemblances to one another. Bernard Suits, in *The Grasshopper: Games, Life and Utopia* (1978), defined playing a game as engaging in activity directed toward a specific state of affairs, using only means permitted by rules that prohibit more efficient in favor of less efficient means; he called the players' acceptance of unnecessary obstacles the lusory attitude. The French sociologist Roger Caillois, in *Les jeux et les hommes* (1961), held that a game is fun, separate in time and place, uncertain in outcome, non-productive, governed by rules, and fictitious. In *Homo Ludens* (1938), Johan Huizinga treated play as a primary force in cultural development.

Games are a universal feature of human culture and have served for entertainment, teaching, ritual, and socialization. The Royal Game of Ur, from [[Mesopotamia]], and Senet, played in [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egypt]], are among the oldest known games, dating to at least 2600 BC; fragments of a Senet board date from about 3100 BC, and a board inscribed for Amenhotep III survives intact. Both were race games and precursors of backgammon. The board game [[Go (game)|Go]] has written accounts as early as the Spring and Autumn period in China, and mancala has Neolithic versions found in Jordan from about 6900 BC. [[Chess]] traces to the [[Gupta Empire]] of India around the 6th century, with chaturanga a likely ancestor; it spread through Persia as chatrang, entered Europe by way of Moorish Spain, and approached its modern form by the 15th century. Playing cards may date to Tang dynasty China (618–907) and reached Europe in the 14th century via the Mamluk Sultanate. Pachisi, played in the Mughal court, underlies Parcheesi and Ludo, and the Aztecs played a race game called patolli.

The 20th century brought mass-market tabletop games such as Monopoly, Scrabble, Clue, and Trivial Pursuit, and the emergence of [[Video game|video games]]; Pong, the first commercially successful arcade video game, appeared in 1972. The video game industry has grown to surpass film and music in annual revenue, and one estimate gives its revenue as $182.7 billion in 2024. Psychologists link play to cognitive development in children and to the absorbed concentration called flow in adults, and [[Game theory|game theory]] uses the structure of games to model decision making in economics and evolutionary biology.

Trans-boundary river of South Asia, 2,525 km long, flowing through India and Bangladesh. Known as the Ganga in India and the Padma in Bangladesh, it rises in the western [[Himalayas]] in the Indian state of [[Uttarakhand]] and flows south and east through the Gangetic plain. Its basin covers approximately 1,114,000 sq km of fertile alluvial plains that support intensive agriculture.

The main stem begins at Devprayag, where the Alaknanda and the Bhagirathi meet. The Alaknanda is longer and thus the source stream in hydrology, while the Bhagirathi, which rises at Gomukh at 4,356 m, is considered the source in Hindu mythology. At [[Prayagraj]] the river joins the 1,444 km-long [[Yamuna]]. The Ghaghara is its largest tributary by discharge. In West Bengal, a feeder canal diverts half of its flow south to the Hooghly River. In Bangladesh the river, renamed the Padma, is joined by the Jamuna and the Meghna, forming the Ganges Delta and emptying into the [[Bay of Bengal]]. The Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna system is the second-largest river system on earth by discharge.

The river is a lifeline to hundreds of millions of people, and many former imperial capitals lie on its banks or those of its tributaries. It is home to approximately 140 species of fish and 90 species of amphibians, including the critically endangered [[Gharial|gharial]]. It is the most sacred river to followers of [[Hinduism]], who worship it as the goddess Ganga.

The Ganges is severely polluted: fecal coliform bacteria near [[Varanasi]] exceed the Indian government's official limit by more than 100 times. The Ganga Action Plan, a cleanup initiative, has been considered a failure, with causes variously attributed to corruption, government inattention, poor technical expertise and planning, and a lack of support from religious authorities.

Planned space, usually outdoors, set aside for the cultivation, display, and enjoyment of plants and other forms of nature. The single feature identifying even the wildest wild garden is control. Some are purely ornamental, while others also produce food crops. Food-producing gardens differ from farms in their smaller scale, more labor-intensive methods, and purpose: enjoyment of a pastime or self-sustenance rather than sale.

The term was traditionally more general; [[Zoo|zoos]] were formerly called zoological gardens. Western gardens are almost universally based on plants, but some traditional eastern types, such as Zen gardens, use plants sparsely or not at all. [[Landscape architecture]] is a related profession. The word derives from Middle English *gardin*, of Germanic origin, akin to Old High German *gart*, an enclosure, as in [[Stuttgart]]; all its cognates refer to a defined enclosed space. In British English a garden is a small enclosed area usually adjoining a building, which American English calls a yard.

The earliest recorded Chinese gardens were created in the valley of the [[Yellow River]] during the [[Shang dynasty]] (1600–1046 BC). They were large, enclosed parks where kings and nobles hunted game or where fruit and vegetables were grown. Inscriptions from this period carry three characters for garden: *yòu*, a royal garden for birds and animals; *pǔ*, a garden for plants; and *yuán*, which during the [[Qin dynasty]] (221–206 BC) became the character for all gardens. During the [[Spring and Autumn period]] (722–481 BC), the Terrace of Gusu, begun in 505 BC, was built on a mountainside with terraces connected by galleries and a lake on which boats shaped like blue dragons sailed. In India, *Manasollasa*, a 12th-century [[Sanskrit]] text, details garden design. Gardens have also embodied ideals of paradise, as in the Persian *pairidaeza*, an enclosed park that influenced the English word "paradise".

State of matter with neither fixed volume nor fixed shape, a compressible form of fluid. A pure gas consists of individual atoms, as in a [[Noble gas|noble gas]] such as neon, or of molecules, such as oxygen (O₂) or carbon dioxide; pure gases can also be mixed, as in air. What distinguishes gases from liquids and solids is the vast separation of the individual particles, which makes some gases invisible. The gaseous state lies between the liquid and [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]] states.

The only elements that are stable diatomic molecular gases at standard temperature and pressure are hydrogen (H₂), nitrogen (N₂), oxygen (O₂), fluorine (F₂), and chlorine (Cl₂). In the atmosphere, nitrogen makes up about 78% and oxygen about 21%.

The word was first used in the early 17th century by the Brabantian chemist Jan Baptist van Helmont, who identified carbon dioxide, the first known gas other than air. It appears to be a phonetic transcription of the Greek *chaos*, following alchemical usage first attested in the works of [[Paracelsus]].

Gases are described by four macroscopic properties: pressure, volume, number of particles, and temperature. [[Robert Boyle]] trapped gas in the closed end of a J-shaped tube with a column of mercury and found that as pressure increased the volume decreased, the product of the two remaining constant. Such observations by Boyle, Jacques Charles, John Dalton, Joseph Gay-Lussac, and Amedeo Avogadro led to the [[Ideal gas law|ideal gas law]]. Because the particles are widely separated, gases have weaker [[Intermolecular force|intermolecular forces]] than liquids or solids, low [[Density|density]] and [[Viscosity|viscosity]], and diffuse to distribute themselves evenly throughout any container. According to kinetic molecular theory, the particles move in continuous random motion and exert pressure on their container through elastic collisions.

Inflammation of the [[Gastrointestinal tract|gastrointestinal tract]], including the stomach and intestine, also known as infectious diarrhea. Symptoms include diarrhea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, and may include fever and dehydration. Signs usually begin 12–72 hours after infection and typically last less than two weeks. Although it is unrelated to [[Influenza|influenza]], it is often called "stomach flu" in Canada and the United States.

The disease is usually caused by viruses, though bacteria, parasites, and fungi can also be responsible. In children, [[Rotavirus|rotavirus]] is the most common cause of severe disease; in adults, [[Norovirus|norovirus]] and *Campylobacter* are common causes. Norovirus accounts for about 90% of viral gastroenteritis outbreaks among adults in America, which occur where groups of people spend time close together, as on a [[Cruise ship|cruise ship]]. The disease spreads through improperly prepared food, contaminated water, or close contact with an infected person.

Dehydration is a common complication. Reactive arthritis follows about 1% of *Campylobacter* infections and Guillain–Barré syndrome 0.1%. Repeated infections, typical where sanitation is poor and malnutrition common, can cause stunted growth and long-term cognitive delays.

Treatment centers on fluids: oral rehydration solution for mild or moderate cases, and intravenous fluids for severe ones. Continued [[Breastfeeding|breastfeeding]] is recommended for breastfed infants and [[Zinc|zinc]] supplementation for children. [[Antibiotic|Antibiotics]] are generally not needed, except for young children with fever and bloody diarrhea. Prevention includes hand washing with soap, clean water, and proper disposal of human waste, and the rotavirus vaccine is recommended for children.

In 2021 there were 4.67 billion cases and 1.17 million deaths worldwide. Children and people in the developing world are affected most; in 2011 there were about 1.7 billion cases, causing about 700,000 deaths of children under five. Adults are less affected, partly because of acquired immunity.

Range of social, psychological, cultural, and behavioral aspects of being a man (or boy), woman (or girl), or portraying a third gender. Gender often corresponds to sex, though a [[Transgender|transgender]] person may identify with a gender other than the sex assigned at birth. Most cultures have a gender binary; those outside it may fall under the umbrella term [[Non-binary|non-binary]]. Some societies have third genders, such as the hijras of [[South Asia]] and two-spirit persons native to North America.

The English word comes from [[Middle English]] *gender*, from Anglo-Norman and Middle French *gendre*, from [[Latin]] *genus*, meaning "kind", "type", or "sort". Before the mid-20th century it was uncommon to use it for anything but grammatical categories. A distinction between biological sex and gender then developed in psychology, sociology, sexology, and [[Feminism|feminism]], and in the 1970s feminist scholars adopted it to separate "socially constructed" aspects of male–female differences from "biologically determined" ones. Most contemporary social scientists in Western countries, many biologists, many legal systems, and the WHO make this distinction.

The subject is contested. Critics of the sex-gender distinction argue that it obscures the biological reality of sex, which they define by the two gamete types, and that policies prioritizing gender identity disadvantage women in athletics. Supporters of gender-identity-inclusive policies respond that the distinction reflects real differences between bodily traits and social roles or identity, and that inclusion can be balanced with fairness through eligibility rules. Reported prevalence of gender dysphoria has risen among youth since the early 2010s; proposed explanations include greater social acceptance, peer and online influence, and changes in clinical practice, and their relative weight is disputed. The social sciences often treat gender as a social construct, while the natural sciences investigate how far biology shapes it. Estimates of how common [[Intersex|intersex]] conditions are range from about 0.018% of births to about 1.7%, depending on definition.

Basic unit of heredity in biology, with two meanings. The Mendelian gene is the classical unit of heredity and refers to any heritable trait; in *The Selfish Gene*, [[Richard Dawkins]] argues that it is the unit of evolution. The molecular gene, the sense more common in biochemistry and molecular biology, is a sequence of nucleotides in [[DNA]] that is transcribed to produce [[RNA]]. There are two types: protein-coding genes and non-coding genes. During [[Gene expression|gene expression]], DNA is first copied into RNA, which can be directly functional or serve as the template for synthesis of a protein.

Genes and their regulatory sequences are mainly responsible for determining an organism's physical traits, or phenotype. A gene can acquire [[Mutation|mutations]], producing variants known as alleles that may be expressed as different traits. Populations evolve when allele frequencies shift, mostly through [[Natural selection|natural selection]] and [[Genetic drift|genetic drift]].

Early work in molecular genetics suggested that one gene makes one protein. Genes producing repressor RNAs were proposed in the 1950s, and by the 1960s textbooks included noncoding genes for functional RNAs such as ribosomal RNA and transfer RNA. Most definitions treat a gene as a transcription unit and regard regulatory sequences as controlling expression without being part of the gene; Kostas Kampourakis emphasizes that a gene must encode a functional product, so transcribed pseudogenes and transcription noise do not qualify. Some publications still restrict the term to protein-coding genes.

The discovery of introns in the 1970s showed that many eukaryotic genes are much larger than their functional products imply. Typical mammalian protein-coding genes are about 62,000 base pairs long in the transcribed region, and since there are about 20,000 of them they occupy about 35–40% of the mammalian genome. In the [[Human genome|human genome]], the approximately 19,000 to 20,000 protein-coding genes make up about 1.5% of the total DNA sequence.

Branch of biology concerned with the study of [[Gene|genes]], genetic variation, and heredity in organisms. The Moravian Augustinian friar [[Gregor Mendel]], working in Brno in the 19th century, was the first to study it scientifically. In a paper presented in 1865 he traced the inheritance of certain traits in pea plants, described the patterns mathematically, and showed that organisms inherit traits through discrete "units of inheritance". His work gained wide understanding only in 1900, when Hugo de Vries and other scientists rediscovered it. William Bateson, a proponent of Mendel's work, coined the word *genetics* in 1905, from the Greek *genesis*, "origin".

Heredity had been used since prehistoric times to improve crop plants and animals through selective breeding. Among earlier theories were blending inheritance, implied by [[Charles Darwin]]'s *On the Origin of Species* (1859), and the inheritance of acquired characteristics, commonly associated with [[Jean-Baptiste Lamarck]] and now known to be wrong. Mendel's results showed that traits are produced by combinations of distinct genes rather than a continuous blend.

[[James Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]] modeled DNA as a double helix in 1953, and the genetic code was cracked in the 1960s. The Human Genome Project (1990–2003) sequenced approximately 99% of the [[Human genome|human genome]] to high accuracy.

Modern genetics studies gene structure, function, variation, and distribution in the cell, the organism, and the population. Its subfields include molecular genetics, [[Epigenetics|epigenetics]], population genetics, and paleogenetics, and the organisms studied span archaea, bacteria, and eukarya. Genetic processes work with an organism's environment and experiences to influence development and behavior, often called nature versus nurture. In a classic example, two genetically identical corn seeds, one grown in a temperate climate and one in an arid climate, differ in height: the plant in the arid climate grows to only half the height of the other because of lack of water and nutrients.
